articles.body: A file ending in ".svg" is not automatically a good production asset. A traced logo can look fine in a preview and still have broken counters, unwanted background shapes, or outlines that are painful to edit. I'm Bilal, the founder of Pixel2Vector. Instead of another product introduction, here is a practical checklist you can use with any raster-to-vector workflow. 1. Start with the right source Before converting, ask whether the original vector already exists. An SVG, PDF, or design source from the creator is usually a better starting point than tracing a small screenshot. If raster is all you have: Use the clearest original available, not an image repeatedly sent through messaging apps. Crop unrelated content without cutting into the artwork.

articles.title: Your upscaler's best PSNR can belong to the frame that looks broken
articles.excerpt: I spent an afternoon trying to answer a question that sounded simple: when a before upscaling or after? This post is about that instrument. The crop-order result is real, but the more A 960×720 pictur…
articles.body: I spent an afternoon trying to answer a question that sounded simple: when a video has black bars, should you crop them before upscaling or after ? Everyone crops first. I did too. But I wanted the number that proves it, and the number turned out to be a bad choice of instrument. This post is about that instrument. The crop-order result is real, but the more useful finding is that PSNR — the metric you'd naturally reach for — is structurally blind to this class of error, and there is one cheap check that catches it. The setup A 960×720 picture inside a 1280×720 frame: 160 px of black bar on each side. That's a 16:9 picture in a 4:3 frame, which is what happens the moment you letterbox anything for an old display, a vertical platform, or a fixed-aspect player.

articles.title: io_uring vs epoll: Paying Per Syscall or Paying in Complexity
articles.excerpt: A server that handles a million requests per second is not really doing a million units of work. It is doing a million units of work plus the cost of telling the kernel about each one, and at that sca…
articles.body: A server that handles a million requests per second is not really doing a million units of work. It is doing a million units of work plus the cost of telling the kernel about each one, and at that scale the telling dominates. epoll has been the answer since 2002: register the sockets once, then ask which ones are ready. io_uring, merged in Linux 5.1, asks a different question — why tell the kernel anything at all, when you can drop requests into a shared ring and let it pick them up? epoll costs roughly three syscalls per request, which at a million requests per second is three million mode switches and about half a core; io_uring with submission polling can drive the same load with zero syscalls per request, at the price of a kernel-version and security-policy matrix.
articles.author: gxqwb

articles.title: QUIC vs TCP with TLS 1.3: Buying Latency with CPU
articles.excerpt: Every few years the transport layer gets rebuilt, and every rebuild makes the same trade: move complexity out of the kernel and into the application, then pay for it in cycles per byte. QUIC is the cu…
articles.body: Every few years the transport layer gets rebuilt, and every rebuild makes the same trade: move complexity out of the kernel and into the application, then pay for it in cycles per byte. QUIC is the current version of that trade. It folds the TLS handshake into the transport handshake, gives every stream its own delivery guarantee, and runs entirely in userspace over UDP. TCP with TLS 1.3 keeps the kernel fast path and the middlebox ecosystem that has grown around it for forty years. QUIC saves one round trip at connection setup and removes transport head-of-line blocking, but it moves packet processing into userspace, where a single core handles roughly one to three gigabits per second instead of ten or more. Part One: What is being compared TCP with TLS 1.3 is two handshakes stacked.

articles.title: Astronomers discover rare black holes that formed when stars failed to go supernova
articles.excerpt: Gravitational waves have revealed a population of black holes that may have been born when masssive stars failed to go supernova.
articles.body: Gravitational waves have revealed a population of black holes that may have been born when masssive stars failed to go supernova. Most of us know the origin story of black holes , or we thought we did. Massive stars run out of the fuel for nuclear fusion and their cores collapse. As this happens, the stars' outer layers expand outwards. Shockwaves from the core collapse strike the outer layers, triggering a supernova explosion. The collapsed core creates a black hole. However, new research based on gravitational wave data collected by LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) and its gravitational wave detector partners, Virgo and KAGRA (Kamioka Gravitational Wave Detector), suggests this might not be the complete picture of black hole birth.

articles.body: The failure of a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying a full load of internet satellites for Amazon was caused by an anomaly in its first-stage booster, rocket maker United Launch Alliance said today (Nov. 17). That failure — which led to the loss of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites — was recognized about 10 minutes after liftoff, but the problems began much earlier than that, ULA said in a statement. "While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit," ULA wrote in today's update .

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 17, 1967: NASA's Surveyor 6 moon probe makes 1st-ever successful launch and hop from the lunar surface
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 17, 1967, NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft made the first liftoff from the lunar surface. Here's how it helped Apollo astronauts.
articles.body: On Nov. 17, 1967, NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft made the first liftoff from the lunar surface. Surveyor 6 was one of several robotic lunar missions NASA sent to scout the moon before sending humans there. It took television pictures of the surface and learned about the composition of lunar soil. Then came the big liftoff. First Surveyor 6 launched from the surface and hopped to another position about 8 feet (2 meters) away. Next, Surveyor 6 took pictures of its original landing site. Flight controllers on Earth could see the landing pad prints of Surveyor 6. They also saw an imprint from the rocket exhaust when Surveyor 6 lifted off. Surveyor 6 showed that spacecraft could land on the moon, and lift off again. Less than two years later, humans did the same thing during Apollo 11 .

articles.title: NICER Status Updates
articles.excerpt: November 17, 2026 NASA’s NICER Telescope Ends Science Operations After studying the universe for six and a half years beyond its initial mission, NASA’s NICER (Neutron star Interior Composition Explor…
articles.body: November 17, 2026 NASA’s NICER Telescope Ends Science Operations After studying the universe for six and a half years beyond its initial mission, NASA’s NICER (Neutron star Interior Composition Explorer) telescope on the International Space Station has ended science operations.  The mission and space station teams are now focused on plans to finalize NICER’s 8-year archive of X-ray science observations and decommission and detach the telescope from its perch near the station’s starboard solar array. In June 2025, NICER was suddenly unable to swivel side-to-side beyond its current orientation, which limited its ability to track cosmic objects. The team paused data collection to investigate the issue.

articles.body: Editor’s Note: This article was originally published on Oct. 15, 2026, and has been updated to correct the location and update the duration of the flight deployment. A NASA Dynamic Aviation A200 aircraft will conduct low-flying research flights over farmland near Amarillo, Texas, from Thursday, Oct. 22, through Monday, Nov. 2. These flights will measure gaseous and particulate emissions from animal feeding operations. A photo of the Dynamic Aviation A200 aircraft, which will conduct low-flying research flights over farmland near Amarillo, Texas, to measure emissions in October and November 2026. Dynamic Aviation Agricultural emissions represent an important and understudied part of Earth’s land and atmosphere systems.
